This is a fantastic roguelike with some truly unique and innovative mechanics that make it a novel standout in the genre. It simplifies a lot of the typical monotony of going through menus in favor of immediately equipping better equipment when you pick it up and auto selling inferior equipment to the merchant as well. The systems are very streamlined but at the same time every run feels completely different due to the different disguises giving totally different foundations for characters which will then be further differentiated by which grimoires you find for spells, the stat choices you make leveling up, which potions you find, etc. 

Juggling human and vampire form is a genuine task, there are many benefits to staying a vamp like being physically superior, healing off of enemy blood (so combat leads directly to your heal condition), not needing to worry about the limited food resource, not having the vampires attack you in the hotel, etc.. but all the humans will attack you, your HP slowly drains if you don't have blood, sunlight will RUIN you (and the game has a day / night cycle with looots of windows in the hotel) and you lose all access to your spells (though vamps can get their own abilities).. this all adds up to a constant tug-o-war between human / vamp form I really like in practice. You're always wondering if you want to waste a soul elixir to turn back human or just trudge on further, or panicking because you don't have an elixir and it's almost daybreak.. there's a timer that always ticks down bringing you closer to vamping out so you can't stay human forever. I really like how they implemented this mechanic, balancing your time between both forms is very important to success in this game which makes GKH stand apart from other roguelikes just by itself.. but there's a lot of other cool stuff going on under the hood.

This isn't a super deep, complex roguelike that'll take you 500H just to beat once, but it has very engaging, fun and tactical gameplay with enough depth to keep it all together.. the gameplay loop of this one is probably one of the best I've seen in the genre and it always leaves you ready to start a new run when you die.. which you will be doing a LOT by the way as this game does not pull its punches. I'd give this one a solid 9.5/10, it's a phenomenal game.

Golden Krone Hotel is an indie roguelike that breathes new life into a classic genre through atmosphere, mechanics, and elegant design. Developed and published by Vulgat, it blends gothic horror with traditional dungeon-crawling in a way that feels both familiar and fresh. Set within the walls of a decaying vampire stronghold turned hotel, the game drops players into a grim world of shifting light, transformation, and constant risk. It takes the procedural unpredictability of roguelikes and injects it with a unique thematic twist: you’re not just fighting vampires—you might become one yourself. This interplay between hunter and monster defines the experience, giving each run a sense of narrative and mechanical tension that few roguelikes achieve.

From the outset, Golden Krone Hotel establishes a brooding and mysterious tone. The setting—a labyrinthine hotel ruled by darkness and corruption—is rendered in stark pixel art that perfectly captures its gothic sensibility. The visuals are simple yet evocative, using light and shadow as not just stylistic flourishes but vital gameplay mechanics. The dynamic lighting system is at the heart of the game’s design: as a human, you rely on sunlight and illumination to burn your undead foes, but once you transform into a vampire, the very light that once protected you becomes your greatest danger. This duality infuses every encounter with tension, forcing players to constantly adapt their strategy to the environment and their own shifting state. The lighting doesn’t just decorate the world—it defines how you survive in it.

The gameplay follows the traditional roguelike formula of turn-based exploration, randomized levels, and permadeath, but it distinguishes itself through its emphasis on accessibility and elegant mechanics. Movement and combat are simple to grasp, and the interface avoids the genre’s usual bloat of obscure commands and sprawling inventories. Despite its simplicity, each decision carries weight. Managing your resources, spells, and health while navigating the interplay between light and darkness makes for a deep tactical experience. The potion system, in particular, showcases smart design: instead of random effects that punish experimentation, potions are chosen from a limited set of possibilities, allowing players to take calculated risks without blind guesswork. This careful balance between unpredictability and control makes the game fair without sacrificing tension—a hallmark of good roguelike design.

A defining feature of Golden Krone Hotel is its transformation mechanic. Throughout the game, the player can be infected with vampirism, permanently altering abilities, strengths, and weaknesses. This change is not just cosmetic; it fundamentally redefines the way you engage with the world. As a human, you rely on sunlight, firearms, and spells to defeat monsters. As a vampire, you gain immense power, enhanced senses, and regenerative capabilities—but you must avoid light at all costs. This shift creates a fascinating dynamic that feels like playing two different games in one. Each form has its own rhythm, rewards, and dangers, making every run feel fresh depending on how you adapt. The mechanic also deepens the game’s thematic resonance, turning the player’s own survival instinct into a source of moral and strategic ambiguity. Becoming the monster you set out to destroy is not just a twist—it’s the game’s central philosophical idea.

The atmosphere of Golden Krone Hotel is further elevated by its sound and pacing. The music is sparse but evocative, using subtle tones that build a sense of isolation and dread. Each floor of the hotel feels different—some are cold and sterile, others claustrophobic and labyrinthine—and the procedural generation keeps exploration unpredictable without sacrificing coherence. The writing is brief yet effective, with bits of lore scattered throughout that hint at the cursed history of the hotel and its monstrous denizens. It doesn’t overwhelm the player with exposition, but it provides enough mystery to keep curiosity alive. The result is a roguelike that feels narratively alive, even without a traditional story structure.

While the game’s design is deliberately streamlined, this simplicity also highlights its few shortcomings. Runs are relatively short compared to larger roguelikes, and once the core mechanics are mastered, some players may find the progression curve modest. The procedural levels, though functional, can occasionally feel repetitive in structure, and the pool of enemies and items, while thematically fitting, is not vast. Yet these limitations are offset by the game’s clarity of focus. Rather than attempting to overwhelm the player with endless systems and grind-heavy complexity, Golden Krone Hotel refines its ideas into something tight and purposeful. It’s not a game about endless depth—it’s a game about deliberate, meaningful challenge within a perfectly measured framework.

Golden Krone Hotel stands out as a rare roguelike that manages to be both accessible to newcomers and rewarding to veterans. It distills the essence of the genre—permadeath, tension, tactical choice—into a gothic package brimming with atmosphere and ingenuity. Its use of light and darkness as both mechanic and metaphor is exceptional, and its dual nature system gives every run narrative weight and mechanical depth. It may be small in scale, but it achieves something remarkable: it makes every decision feel dangerous, every victory earned, and every death instructive. For players who love roguelikes but tire of unnecessary complexity, or for those who simply crave a clever, haunting twist on classic design, Golden Krone Hotel is a hidden gem—an elegant descent into the shadows where survival means constantly walking the line between the hunter and the monster.

This is a very pleasant and simple traditional roguelike. It takes many of its levels and enemies from other traditional roguelike classics, but adds interesting vampirism and daytime cycle mechanics to the formula, which give it a distinct character and individuality. Straightforward controls, no inventory management, no wands to worry about, best equipment autoequips, and the usual potion identifying minigame is much more manageable due to the game showing you three potion types that any particular unidentified potion could possibly be. Fun and easy to git gud at, at least on the normal difficulty. An easy recommendation, especially at its price.

Some negatives: the lorebooks, while numerous, are not very interesting; it is sometimes difficult to see items behind other items, for example, potions behind window panes along the bottom of the map; normal difficulty feels too easy after a few runs (i feel i could get long winstreaks pretty easily), while "despair" difficulty feels too hard (only won once after dozens of attempts) -- i wish there was something in-between; and despite there being a website that keeps track of all the high scores, including weeklies, getting a high score does not seem very fun: once you have a good enough character, you can seemingly grind for score forever.

I started playing this game because people on reddit recommended it as a traditional roguelike for people who are either unfamiliar with the genre, or who find the demands of learning a trad roguelike to be offputting (me). This game is streamlined in a beautiful way and while I'm sure it leads to its own issues, it's a very pleasant experience. You can use just keyboard, just controller, just mouse, or a combination. 

You don't need to micro-manage the items you pick up, the game manages them for you automatically. Reading bits of lore you pick up is purely optional. Engaging with the story is mostly done by talking to NPCs, which I largely skip but I like that A) the option is there for players who want to see more of the world and B) it's non-essential for players like me.

This is clearly the work of a developer who loves the genre, understands what makes it fun, and wants to provide the easiest entry possible. I've played 14 hours and I've gotten a few wins so far, all on Easy, but it is a difficult game even then. Its difficulty challenges your decision-making in a way that feels fair and rewarding. I can't remember feeling like I've lost a run due purely to luck, it has almost always been some sort of mistake or misunderstanding on my part.

I've encountered no bugs, everything just works. It's remarkably easy to get into and I would absolutely recommended it for anyone with an interest in this kind of game. If you're a hardcore traditional rougelike player, this game's systems may be less sophisticated than you're used to. That could be a deal-breaker for some but I still think, if you like the genre, this one is worth trying.

It's a good roguelike and well polished by a developer who is obviously a solid student of game design, but regrettably I think it's just a little bit too short and lacking in depth to be satisfying for me as a "traditional" roguelike, speaking as a longtime fan of the genre. I understand this was no doubt an intentional design choice, but I must say I found myself missing the epic adventure part of rogueliking while playing Golden Krone Hotel even as I was very much enjoying not having my ass kicked quite so frequently as would be normal. You may find yourself missing this a little bit too if you are a fan of the oldschool. It's a title that's more approachable for a new generation and a new era, for better and for worse. 

The part that's better is the fact that it really is supremely approachable. The part that's worse is the reality that while you might be deluded into believing you've had a special little world generated for you in Golden Krone Hotel (as is one of the principle charms of the genre), the reality is that you are having an experience very much similar to many other players before you, the procedural generation is not quite deep enough for the principle game play experience to truly vary. To me it feels kinda roguelite minus the meta progression somehow, rather than a trad roguelike. If you are looking for a modern roguelike experience with a low barrier to entry, this will scratch the itch, but I don't think it's going to carve out a legendary space in anyone's lifetime gaming history like say the effort of getting into ADOM or ToME. 

So it's worth a look for fans of the genre, people interested but having a hard time "getting" it, and for students of game design. Doubtful it will take the place of one of the majors in the play rosters of long-term fans, but I also don't think there's anything wrong with that. Not every experience has to be one for a lifetime, and I think it's just the reality that this is more one of those titles that you play for a while and it's great fun but the inevitable depth trade offs surrounding a low barrier to entry also mean it doesn't quite have the secret sauce for the truly legendary moments that the more brutal and unapproachable titles do (nor, in very much a good way, the same frustrations). Definitely worth the price.

Fight vampires or be a vampire. Probably both. A roguelike in the truest turn-based sense, you ascend the steps of the Golden Krone, encountering various creatures, ne'er-do-wells, and other treasure hunters. Coolest thing about being vampire: lopping up blood pools to heal. Coolest thing about the sun: it casts rays through the stained glass that move as the day progresses, killing vampires dumb enough to be overtaken by it (sometimes that's you). Coolest thing about potions: they're unidentified at first, but you're a dabbling alchemist so you have some idea what a potion COULD do (either heal me or explode, screw it I'm drinking it). Coolest thing about the magic system: Only humans can cast spells, and often you can choose between learning a new spell, improving an existing spell, or just gaining mana. Coolest thing about the map: it's not linear, you can dead end up a tower or find the stairs to the sewer.  Underrated gem if you're a roguephile.

There's a reason why GKH is often listed as a top game for getting people into the grid-based, turn-based traditional roguelike genre. It's probably one of the best gateway games to things like Brogue, Cogmind, or Tales of Maj'eyal!

This game rocks and it's a crime it isn't getting more attention! It's a perfectly sized mini roguelike that can be played in an hour or two that's suitably crunchy and tactical without taking tens of hours to learn. Think DoomRL in terms of size and scope.

You are a vampire returning to the hotel owned by Fane, the boss vampire who originally turned your PC into a vampire. There's nine main levels plus multiple side branches — kind of like Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup compressed into a 90 minute experience. You can transform back and forth between vampire and human over the course of the run, and there's a cool "faction" system where humans will mostly leave you alone when you are human, other vamps are friendly when you are in vamp mode.  

As a human, there's an upgradable sword and revolver and a magic system with up to four spells available at a time. In vampire mode you lose the finesse to use weapons and cast spells, but you have a powerful natural claw attack, and regenerate health from enemies that bleed. There's also demon blood which gives vampires spell like abilities which cost HP instead of mana.

Art style is fun and atmospheric and awesome chiptune soundtrack. There's a lot I like about this game!

A fun traditional roguelike, with plenty of "disguises" (the classes of this game) for many different starts. The game sees you going through multiple floors to confront the boss vampire at the top of a tower, requiring you to acquire rings from bosses on the side paths to reach the final floor. The layout of maps is randomized, aside of a few special exceptions, along with randomized spell books and potions adding to replayability. 
You can play focused on melee or spells, with a gun being a ranged attack limited by bullets to complement either playstyle. The unique mechanic for this game is the character is a vampire, and can only remain human while drinking Soul Elixirs (one of the randomized potions, although a common one). Humans can read books for either stat increases or new spells but need to eat, while vampire form can hit harder and see in the dark, but can't use spells, and slowly loses health, regaining health by drinking blood that drops from your enemies. Human Npcs are friendly with the player in human form, and vamps with a player in vamp form.

Overall, there's some fun balancing with the human and vampire forms, and melee or spells are viable, or even both if you found enough stat books. It's not too hard to become overpowered in the end game, and there is a side area that leads to limitless floors. I would recommend to anyone wanting to try a chill roguelike to either relax to if you are a veteran of the genre, or learn this kind of game if you are a newbie.

I really enjoy Golden Krone Hotel.

In Golden Krone hotel you play as a vampire.  You can change between vampire and human forms using either soul elixirs (vampire->human) or blood (human->vampire).  Each form has its advantages and disadvantages - as a human, you can use magical skills and equipment and can regenerate health, but must consume food.  As a vampire, you cannot cast spells or use equipment but you have significantly stronger melee skills and can regain health by hitting enemies and drinking their blood.

You must collect rings of power which then unlocks the final boss.  The rings of power are guarded by mini-bosses in branches, some of which you can only kill in either vampire or human modes.  This creates an interesting challenge and so you have to be conscious of how powerful you are in both forms.  

In each run you will get a branch dedicated to the provision of food.  I like this as it guarantees that you'll have enough food to complete a run, yet also ensures that you only have access to the food by making progress through the levels.  

There's a good variety of spells that you can learn.  There's utility spells such as levitation, which allows you to reach potions and equipment otherwise unreachable.  There's many damage spells such as firestorm, which does fire damage to all surrounding tiles, a spell which creates water tiles, which you can then turn to ice to do damage, a poison ranged spell and many more.  I liked that your character can only have 4 spells and that you are only given a limited selection of spells each time you're offered one, so you need to think about how you want your character build to work given the choices at the time.

There are many potions you can pick up.  Some are very powerful like Big Form.  Some are positive depending on context e.g. a summon creatures potion is negative, but could be positive if you have the Charm spell or if you are a vampire and need blood.  Potions need to be identified via consuming or via an identification scroll (called a 'primer'), but unlike other roguelikes where you must identify everything, all potions are randomly grouped into threes and the game will automatically identify potions that can be deduced from what's left.  This reduces the tedium that some people experience with identification systems.

The tile graphics are beautiful and have a pixel retro appeal.  The music tracks are well done and fit the vampiric theme.  The sound effects are the weakest aspect of the audio visuals but they do the job and do complement the pixel retro graphics.  The user interface for the most part is very clean and easy to use.  The only slightly awkward part is for viewing enemy abilities and resistances - you need to hit the V key then move a cursor on top of an enemy and then hit enter (update - the developer mentioned that you can just right click - certainly easier!). Other than that, all other actions are easy to perform.

Golden Krone Hotel is a pretty forgiving, fun and perhaps relaxing roguelike to play versus its peers.  It certainly does help if you kill vampires via light and flames, but it also doesn't stop you from just stabbing stuff to death with your sword.  You can finish a game in one or two hours once you've learnt all that it has to offer.  I recommend the game to people who enjoy roguelikes - it's not the most complicated roguelike out there but it has many skills and spells to play around with, the asthetics are very nice, the human->vampire system works well and the game is a lot of fun.
